slides.title: Pregnancy: confirmation and routine tests
bullets: hCG is made by the placenta; a pregnancy test finds hCG in urine or blood. Routine tests are done at the first prenatal visit and throughout pregnancy.

slides.title: Pregnancy: confirmation and routine tests
rows: A urine test is about 97–99% accurate 1–2 weeks after a missed period. Quantitative blood hCG is used very early, to monitor high-risk pregnancies and to check for ectopic or molar pregnancy; in early pregnancy hCG roughly doubles every 3 days.
One of the first prenatal visit tests.
In every pregnancy, preferably in the first trimester, regardless of vaccination or prior testing.
All pregnant women should be tested for HIV as part of prenatal care.
At the first visit — testing for sexually transmitted infections, including syphilis.
CDC recommends hepatitis C screening during each pregnancy.
Immunity to rubella and chickenpox is checked at the first visit.

slides.title: Pregnancy: confirmation and routine tests
rows: A urine test can look for urinary tract infection, diabetes and preeclampsia.
Gestational diabetes screening: at 24–28 weeks per NIDDK (26–28 weeks in the OWH table).
Group B streptococcus test at 36–37 weeks.

slides.title: Pregnancy: confirmation and routine tests
rows: The test may have been too early — repeat in about a week; if two home tests are negative but doubt remains, see a clinician.
Fertility medicines can cause a false positive.

slides.title: Toxoplasma (Toxoplasma gondii) and congenital toxoplasmosis
bullets: The genus Toxoplasma contains one species — Toxoplasma gondii; the definitive host is the cat and other felids (sexual reproduction and oocyst formation occur in the small intestine), and all other animals and humans are intermediate hosts.

Humans are infected through food (meat, milk, eggs) and sick domestic animals (rabbit, cat, dog and others); the parasite pierces the gut wall, travels with lymph and blood to cells of the brain, spinal cord, liver, spleen, kidney and muscle, inflames the tissue and forms cysts.

The foetus may be infected from the mother: the child may be born prematurely or dead, and the nervous system, eyes and other organs may be damaged; a live-born child develops slowly mentally and physically.
Acquired acute toxoplasmosis may resemble typhoid: fever, sore throat, enlarged liver and spleen, sometimes damage to the nervous system.

slides.title: Toxoplasma (Toxoplasma gondii) and congenital toxoplasmosis
bullets: Chronic toxoplasmosis: long-lasting high body temperature, pain in the head, throat and muscles, enlarged lymph nodes and liver; the disease may also be latent.
As prevention the book names keeping domestic animals under sanitary control and medical examination of pregnant women.

slides.title: The ELISA method: principle and steps
bullets: ELISA is an immunodiagnostic method that detects a known antibody or antigen through the formation of antigen–antibody immune complexes; it is widely used for hormones, tumour markers, drugs, bacteria, viruses and antibodies against them, and has high sensitivity and strict specificity.
Methods divide into heterogeneous (with a step of mechanically separating free and enzyme-labelled antibodies) and homogeneous.

Steps: the kit reagents, wells with immunosorbent and the sample (serum, plasma) are prepared; the sample is added to the well and incubated at a set temperature, and the unbound part is washed off several times.
A secondary antibody is added — it binds the first antibody and is labelled with an enzyme (peroxidase or alkaline phosphatase); after incubation the excess is washed away.
A colourless substrate is added: the enzyme catalyses a colour-change reaction.

slides.title: The ELISA method: principle and steps
bullets: A stop reagent is added and the optical density of the coloured solution is measured on an ELISA analyser, giving a qualitative and quantitative analysis.

slides.title: PCR diagnostics: principle and use
bullets: PCR (polymerase chain reaction) is the specific amplification of nucleic acids in vitro with synthetic oligonucleotide primers: a particular DNA fragment in the test material is copied many times by the enzyme DNA polymerase, so it can be detected even at a very low concentration.
Primers are usually artificially synthesised oligonucleotides of 15 to 30 nucleotides; well-chosen primers give the analysis its specificity and sensitivity.

PCR is widely used to detect infectious agents, especially when detection by immunological, bacteriological and microscopic methods is poor or impossible; it matters for finding non-growing or hard-to-grow and low-activity forms.

slides.title: PCR diagnostics: principle and use
bullets: Examples in the book: PCR detects hepatitis A, B and C viruses, cytomegalovirus, herpes virus (types 1 and 2), Epstein–Barr virus, Toxoplasma, Chlamydia trachomatis, Gardnerella vaginalis, Candida albicans, mycoplasmas, papillomavirus, Trichomonas vaginalis and others.
Sensitivity: PCR can detect organisms when the sample holds 10–1000 cells (immunological and microscopic tests need 10³–10⁵ cells).

TORCH infections, general description?
bullets: 1. TORCH is a group of infections dangerous to the fetus and newborn in pregnancy: Toxoplasmosis, "Other" (syphilis, varicella, parvovirus B19, Zika, etc.), Rubella, Cytomegalovirus, Herpes simplex.

2. Most dangerous is primary infection during pregnancy (especially rubella – in the first trimester; toxoplasmosis); but 50–75% of congenital CMV occurs in mothers infected before pregnancy (reactivation/reinfection).
3. Consequences: fetal death, congenital malformations (congenital rubella syndrome), hearing loss (CMV), eye and CNS damage (toxoplasmosis, CMV), neonatal herpes.
4. Routes of transmission: transplacental, through the birth canal, after birth (breast milk – CMV).
5. Prevention: rubella vaccination (check immunity before pregnancy), hygiene measures (CMV, toxoplasmosis), screening and targeted testing.

slides.title: Laboratory diagnosis of TORCH infections?
bullets: 1. Serology (ELISA/chemiluminescent): IgG and IgM; IgM alone is not a diagnosis – it persists for months, cross-reactivity and rheumatoid factor give false positives; a large share of positive TORCH IgM results are not confirmed.
2. IgG avidity: low avidity – recent (primary) infection, high – old infection; in toxoplasmosis and CMV interpret with gestational age in mind; confirmation in a reference laboratory.

3. Molecular methods: PCR in amniotic fluid (fetal toxoplasmosis, CMV); in a newborn congenital CMV – PCR in saliva or urine (in the first 2–3 weeks of life; later it cannot be distinguished from postnatal infection), urine for confirmation; IgG/IgM do not confirm congenital CMV.
4. Rubella: serology and PCR (nasopharynx, throat, urine); herpes: PCR from lesions.
5. Dynamics in paired sera (seroconversion) and pre-pregnancy screening results make interpretation easier.

slides.title: Molecular methods in diagnosing infections in pregnant women and newborns?
bullets: 1. Main infections in pregnancy and in newborns: CMV, toxoplasmosis, rubella, herpes, HIV, hepatitis B, etc.
2. Congenital CMV: within 2–3 weeks after birth PCR in saliva (preferred) or urine; a sample taken later cannot distinguish congenital from acquired.
3. Toxoplasmosis: to confirm fetal infection – PCR in amniotic fluid; serology in the mother (IgM, IgG, avidity) is confirmed in a reference laboratory.
4. Rubella: PCR (nasopharynx, urine) and serology; in the first trimester of pregnancy the risk of transmission is high.
5. Advantages of the molecular method: in the newborn maternal IgG antibodies confound serology, PCR detects the pathogen directly; timing and type of specimen are important.
